To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

endothelial cells can sense hemodynamic forces and transduce them via specific signaling pathways into changes in the transcription of genes that encode proteins with important functions in vascular physiology and pathophysiology.

the vascular endothelial lining can discriminate among various fluid mechanical forces and transduce them via specific transcriptional regulatory events into atheroprotective or atherogenic phenotypic changes.

(1) hemodynamic forces are important in determining the phenotype of the endothelium; (2) the phenotype of the vascular endothelum is a key determinant of the susceptibility to atherosclerosis; (3) the phenotype of endothelium is regulated by hemodynamic forces; (4) endothelial dysfunction contributes to atherogenesis; and (5) hemodynamic forces can regulate endothelial function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of endothelial phenotypic modulation in atherogenesis and the mechanisms whereby hemodynamic forces regulate this modulation.

elucidating the mechanisms by which the endothelium senses hemodynamic forces, transduces these stimuli into specific genetic programs, and ultimately regulates the expression of atheroprotective genes.

understanding the mechanisms whereby the endothelium senses and responds to various hemodynamic forces and how such biomechanical signals influence the expression of genes that are relevant to vascular disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hemodynamic forces can modulate the expression of genes in the endothelum and that this can contribute to the development of atherosclerosis.
hemodynamic forces, via their effects on the endothelium, are a major determinant in atherogenesis, but that the mechanisms involved are complex and not fully understood.
the vascular endothelial lining is a dynamic tissue that is exquisitely sensitive to the hemodynamic environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
endothelial cells sense and respond to hemodynamic forces by modulating gene expression in a manner that influences atherogenesis.
the endothelium is a mechanosensor that is capable of transducing hemodynamic signals into genetic regulatory events that can modulate atherogenesis.

the endothelial cells are able to respond to the mechanical forces generated by blood flow, and this response is mediated by the activation of transcription factors that bind to the promoter of genes that regulate endothelial function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
endothelium is a mechanosensor that is capable of transducing the hemodynamic environment into specific patterns of gene expression.
the hemodynamic environment can influence atherogenesis by modulating endothelial gene expression, which, in turn, can affect the balance of pro‐ and anti‐atherogenic factors in the vessel wall.

the endothelium can discriminate among various fluid mechanical stimuli and transduce this information to the level of individual (or multiple) genes, and that the selective expression of certain genes in response to steady laminar flow may play a role in the prevention of atherosclerosis.
